title: UserArena: Benchmarking Interactive User Simulation for Long-Horizon Shopping Agents

details.title: UserArena: Benchmarking Interactive User Simulation for Long-Horizon Shopping Agents
details.abstract: Can simulated shoppers faithfully reproduce real users’ behavior over long shopping interactions? We introduce UserArena , an interactive benchmark grounded in real-world e-commerce data: 64,729 sessions from 11,010 users , covering 566,102 items and 13 action types. Its five-level evaluation goes beyond next-action accuracy to assess sequential behavior, personalization, and outcomes. It also validates offline policy comparisons against a controlled production A/B test. We further propose On-Policy Trajectory Distillation (OPTD) , which uses trajectory-level intent to guide dense token-level teacher supervision on student-generated responses. Among the evaluated simulators, OPTD achieves the strongest overall fidelity and most closely reproduces the policy effect observed in production. 💻 Code & data: https://github.com/RecGPT-Team/UserArena 🌐 Project: https://recgpt-team.github.io/UserArena-Page

title: RSIHub: A Composable Framework for Agent-Evolution Methods

details.title: RSIHub: A Composable Framework for Agent-Evolution Methods
details.abstract: Hi everyone! We’re sharing RSIHub, an open-source framework for building and comparing agent-evolution methods. RSIHub lets researchers compose reusable operators to improve agent prompts, skills, tools, and orchestration, while keeping evaluation protected and candidate histories traceable. We implement AHE, Hyperagents, A-Evolve, and GEPA on shared infrastructure and evaluate them with MiniSWE and Codex on Terminal Bench 2 and τ³ Banking. Our goal is to make agent self-improvement experiments easier to reproduce, compare, and extend. We’d love feedback, contributions, and ideas for new evolution methods and benchmarks! 💻 Code: https://github.com/simple-agent-lab/RSIHub 🌐 Project: https://simpleagentlab.com/rsihub/

title: RynnUnify: Towards Unified Embodied Brain

details.title: RynnUnify: Towards Unified Embodied Brain
details.abstract: Introduction We present RynnUnify , a Mixture-of-Transformers architecture with an autoregressive Reasoner and a rectified-flow video Generator . Built on Cosmos3, RynnUnify connects embodied understanding, spatial grounding, and long-horizon visual planning through interleaved video-language reasoning. Unified Embodied Brain. RynnUnify brings embodied cognition, spatial grounding, and video generation into one architecture, connecting scene understanding with predictions of how the physical world evolves. Interleaved Visual Planning. RynnUnify alternates subtask reasoning with video prediction, using each generated outcome to plan the next step. Cross-chunk scene memory, self-forcing training, and adaptive durations support coherent visual planning over long horizons. Agentic Interleaved Thinking. An RL-trained agent learns when to answer directly and when to generate visual evidence. Through BCPO, it learns to formulate generation requests, interpret predicted outcomes, and select the reasoning path that benefits the task. Connect Prediction to Action. The World-Action Model ( WAM ) extension translates predictive world representations into robot control through joint video-action training, supporting composite manipulation tasks.

title: Echo: Coupled Action and Task Status Signal Denoising for Vision Language Action Models

details.title: Echo: Coupled Action and Task Status Signal Denoising for Vision Language Action Models
details.abstract: Recognizing task completion and failure enables robots to stop upon success and initiate recovery or replanning after failure. Existing methods augment Vision Language Action (VLA) policies with task status signal prediction to support these execution decisions. However, learning and integrating these signals can require fine-grained supervision, external monitoring models, or complex architectural designs. Moreover, the potential of task status signals to directly guide action generation remains underexplored. We present Echo, a framework that combines task status signal learning without frame-level progress annotations with a compact design for status prediction and action generation within a single VLA. Specifically, Echo represents task status with stop and failure signals, added as two dimensions of each action chunk and denoised together with robot actions. Their combination distinguishes ongoing execution, successful completion, and failure. To learn these signals without fine-grained progress annotations, Echo constructs successful, failed, and recovery trajectories with complementary supervision properties. To enable status signal-guided action generation, Echo controls interactions between the signals and actions and denoises the signals faster than the actions. These allow later action denoising steps to condition on cleaner status estimates while preserving accurate signal prediction. Extensive real-world manipulation experiments show that Echo accurately predicts task status and consistently improves policy performance.

title: FLOMSS: Generative Music Source Separation by Flow Matching

details.title: FLOMSS: Generative Music Source Separation by Flow Matching
details.abstract: FLOMSS systematically investigates flow matching for full-band stereo music source separation (MSS). Systematic design study: We investigate prediction targets, flow paths, single- vs. multi-source modeling, and mixture consistency. Optimal Transport-CFM with x-prediction provides the most balanced performance across the evaluated metrics. Beyond SDR: We evaluate MSS with signal-level, spectral, embedding-based, distributional, and subjective metrics, revealing a distributional–reconstruction trade-off: flow-matching models improve spectral and embedding-based similarity while generally sacrificing some SDR. Strong generative MSS performance: FLOMSS-S outperforms prior generative baselines on most spectral and perceptual metrics. Competitive subjective quality: Scaling to FLOMSS-M improves every reported objective metric over FLOMSS-S and ranks #2 overall in the listening test, despite its lower SDR than strong discriminative separators. These results highlight flow matching as a promising direction for generative music source separation with competitive perceptual quality.

details.abstract: Trajectory2Gym is a framework for scaling tool-use agents through compositional coverage and decision-grounded supervision. It constructs executable interactions that capture multi-step dependencies and trains agents on decisions supported by their visible interaction history. Across five Qwen3 model scales, Trajectory2Gym consistently improves performance on τ-bench, τ²-bench, and BFCL, achieving +16.9 to +29.8 percentage points in the average benchmark score.

title: StreamVibe: Proactive Video Agents for Evolving User Intent

details.title: StreamVibe: Proactive Video Agents for Evolving User Intent
details.abstract: Vision-language models are shifting from offline passive understanding toward online proactive interaction. However, prevailing methods largely rely on explicit requests while overlooking implicit user intents (e.g., “where should I click next?” when a user is navigating a website) and fail to continuously update their understanding as user intents evolve. These limitations make them less suitable for intent-aware interaction in real-world scenarios. To address these challenges, we introduce StreamVibe-Bench, a new benchmark that serves as a testbed for user intent understanding and interaction, comprising 4.1K evaluation samples and 85K training samples spanning explicit, implicit, and dynamic intents. Building on this benchmark, we develop StreamVibe-VL, a streaming proactive model that infers implicit user intents from continuous observations and dynamically adapts its interactions as these intents evolve. We further introduce StreamVibe-Harness, which maintains user intents as persistent states with flexible lifecycles through hierarchical memory, enabling it to track the latest user intents and environmental states. Our experiments reveal three key findings: (i) StreamVibe-VL preserves strong general video understanding capabilities while improving response timing and answer quality by 10.7% over existing baselines; (ii) existing proactive models remain limited in understanding user intents and determining when to respond, especially under implicit and dynamic intents; and (iii) StreamVibe-Harness further improves response consistency and adaptation during sustained interactions, resulting in a 12.3% gain in proactive interaction performance.

title: Trial by Trace: Benchmarking AI Agent Harnesses for Reliability and Failure Attribution

details.title: Trial by Trace: Benchmarking AI Agent Harnesses for Reliability and Failure Attribution
details.abstract: Task success does not always mean the agent harness worked reliably. We introduce TraceTrial-Bench, a benchmark that evaluates agent task performance and harness reliability separately, using 95 mechanism-oriented tasks across seven components: context, execution, governance, lifecycle, observability, tools, and verification. Across 4 harnesses, 9 models, and 3,420 runs, 31.1% of runs achieve task success despite failing at least one harness criterion. Our framework combines trajectory tracing, multi-source evidence, and two-layer evaluation to support auditable reliability assessment and evidence-based failure analysis. We welcome feedback from researchers and developers working on agent harnesses, evaluation, and reliability!

title: Continual Learning Exam: Benchmarking Long-Horizon RSI and Experiential Learning in LLM Agents

details.title: Continual Learning Exam: Benchmarking Long-Horizon RSI and Experiential Learning in LLM Agents
details.abstract: 🚀 Introducing Continual Learning Exam (CLE): Benchmarking Long-Horizon RSI and Experiential Learning in LLM Agents! 🧠 Can LLM agents truly learn from experience and continuously improve over time? Most existing agent benchmarks focus on whether agents can solve individual tasks. But real-world intelligence requires more than task completion: agents should learn from past successes and failures, accumulate experience, and transfer acquired knowledge, strategies, and skills to future challenges. To bridge this gap, we introduce Continual Learning Exam (CLE), a large-scale benchmark designed to evaluate long-horizon continual learning and experience-driven self-improvement in LLM agents. 🌟 Key Highlights: 🔹 Built with 50+ domain experts, covering 120 real-world professional tasks, 600 progressive levels, and 89 occupations across 12 domains. 🔹 Realistic professional environments, featuring ~24K real-world files, 19 stateful applications, and 16K+ human-authored evaluation criteria. 🔹 Game-like Task Ladders, where agents must complete each level to unlock the next. Later levels require agents to reuse and build upon knowledge, strategies, and skills acquired through earlier experience. 📊 Key Findings: We evaluated 17 frontier agent configurations. Even the strongest system, Claude Code + Opus 5, achieves only: • 47.7% level completion rate • 23.3% full Task Ladder completion rate These results reveal a substantial gap between solving individual tasks and achieving genuine long-term continual learning. We hope CLE can serve as a realistic and verifiable benchmark to advance research on Agent Continual Learning, Memory, Skill Learning, and Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI). 💡 Beyond Task Solving: Towards Continual Learning and Experience-Driven Self-Improvement. We welcome feedback, discussions, and collaborations from the community!

title: Work Agents: Systems, Capabilities, and Optimization

details.title: Work Agents: Systems, Capabilities, and Optimization
details.abstract: As foundation models evolve from information generation to digital work execution, agents are increasingly capable of completing complex tasks across tools, applications, and workflows. However, existing research lacks a unified perspective on how agents reliably accomplish delegated work. To address this gap, we present a work-centric, system-level perspective that views work agents as systems combining foundation models and runtime harnesses to execute tasks in stateful workspaces and deliver verifiable outcomes. We introduce two complementary dimensions, work persistence and work openness, to characterize working conditions, and classify digital work into five forms according to task scope and organization. Building on this framework, we identify five core capability families required for reliable work execution and examine approaches to model optimization, harness optimization, and their joint optimization. We further analyze existing evaluation methods and metrics from the perspective of work outcomes. Finally, we discuss future research directions, including sustained work delegation, adaptation to open environments, and the interaction between work execution and capability improvement. This paper provides a unified framework for understanding, optimizing, and evaluating work agents, supporting the development of systems capable of delivering reliable, verifiable, and practically valuable work outcomes.

title: ProAS: A Progress-Aware Advantage Shaping Framework for Multi-Turn Agentic Reinforcement Learning

details.title: ProAS: A Progress-Aware Advantage Shaping Framework for Multi-Turn Agentic Reinforcement Learning
details.abstract: We argue against the limitations of the traditional GRPO-type credit assignment, such as (1) the unreasonable reinforcement of unreasonable actions within the positively advantaged trajectory,  and (2) the fact that actions within the negatively advantaged trajectory are penalized with the same magnitude regardless of how much the remaining course deviates. Based on such insights, we propose ``ProAS: A Progress-Aware Advantage Shaping Framework for Multi-Turn Agentic Reinforcement Learning''.   It calibrates the GRPO-type credit assignment and results in the improvement of effectiveness and efficiency under multiple setups.

title: Extreme Compression of Per-Layer Embeddings via Cross-Layer Latent Vector Quantization

details.title: Extreme Compression of Per-Layer Embeddings via Cross-Layer Latent Vector Quantization
details.abstract: Recent work shows that increasing embedding capacity can improve language models, making it a promising direction for scaling. As more capacity goes into embedding tables, extreme compression becomes increasingly important: we want to keep the benefits of larger embeddings while fitting models into limited deployment memory. We study this in Gemma 4, where per-layer embeddings (PLE) account for 35.2% of E4B's parameters. At 100× compression, only about five bytes remain for each token–layer vector. Encoding every vector independently gives each one a tiny code and misses the opportunity to share storage across layers. Our method, OPTIC, gives each token one quantized code shared across all layers. Layer-specific affine decoders reconstruct the different PLE vectors from that shared code. We also fit the representation to its effect after the gate and output projection, so the compression objective reflects how the model actually uses the embeddings. At about 100× PLE compression, OPTIC retains 97.8% of BF16 E4B performance across seven benchmarks, compared with 66.3% for product quantization. Serving BF16 E4B directly from the compact codes reduces GPU memory by 29.7%, with at most 0.40% more wall time on an RTX 4090 with the same 1 GiB KV cache. It also works alongside backbone weight quantization. Paper · Code and method walkthrough · Released 100× PLE artifact

title: Trustworthy Recursive Self-Improvement in the Era of Large Models: Foundation, Risks, Evaluation and Open Challenges

details.title: Trustworthy Recursive Self-Improvement in the Era of Large Models: Foundation, Risks, Evaluation and Open Challenges
details.abstract: AI systems built around large models increasingly use experience and feedback to make persistent changes to models, prompts, memories, tools, and workflows. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) extends this process to inductive biases and to the mechanisms that govern future updates, which can themselves be revised and reused across improvement cycles. Yet self-modification alone does not guarantee trustworthy improvement. Reported gains may reflect flawed evaluations, previously acquired capabilities may deteriorate, and compliance with behavioral constraints may weaken. Compromised artifacts or sensitive information may also persist in successor systems. Changes to improvement mechanisms may invalidate earlier verification results and make human oversight less effective. This survey presents an operational definition and process framework for RSI and organizes the requirements for trustworthy RSI into four interconnected themes: genuine and sustained improvement; behavioral constraints, alignment, and fairness; system security and privacy; and transparency and controllability. We examine these themes from three perspectives: Improvement Validity, Constraint Preservation, and Effective Oversight. This analysis covers improvement diagnosis, proposal generation, proposal evaluation, and update implementation (S1--S4), including the recursive application of these stages to improvement mechanisms (RI). We review risks, safeguards, and evaluation evidence for individual updates, effects inherited by successor systems, and revisions to improvement mechanisms, while distinguishing direct RSI findings from evidence in related systems. Finally, we examine evaluation settings, identify requirements for independent and longitudinal assessment, and discuss applications and open research problems.

title: miniTE: Diagnosing and Bridging the Execution Gap in Native NVFP4 Reinforcement Learning

details.title: miniTE: Diagnosing and Bridging the Execution Gap in Native NVFP4 Reinforcement Learning
details.abstract: 🚀 Can we really train LLMs with native FP4 reinforcement learning — without sacrificing stability? Excited to share miniTE , our open-source framework for stable and efficient native NVFP4 (W4A4) RL! One surprising finding: Same weights + same precision ≠ same policy. Even when both the learner and rollout engine use NVFP4, subtle differences in numerical execution can introduce significant training–inference mismatch and eventually destabilize RL. With miniTE, we tackle this challenge from both numerical and systems perspectives: 🔬 Diagnose & align: Identify cross-engine execution differences and bring training–inference log-probability gaps down to ~1e-8 in our strict-alignment setting. ⚡ Make FP4 actually fast: Optimize native NVFP4 kernels, scaling, and grouped GEMMs, achieving up to 1.39× BF16 learner throughput on 8×B300 GPUs. 📈 Keep learning stable: Demonstrate long-horizon RL on Qwen3-30B-A3B with downstream performance close to BF16. Beyond the results, we're releasing the framework, kernels, diagnostics, and training recipes to make native low-bit RL easier to reproduce and extend. FP4 is not just about using fewer bits — it's about making every bit work. 🔥 📄 Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.23928 💻 Details: https://infix.io/research/miniTE We'd love to hear your thoughts, feedback, and ideas for pushing low-precision RL further!

title: ChronoReplay: One Answer Interface Is Not Enough for Streaming Spatial Intelligence

details.title: ChronoReplay: One Answer Interface Is Not Enough for Streaming Spatial Intelligence
details.abstract: ChronoReplay is a training framework designed to improve the spatial reasoning capabilities of streaming vision-language models (VLMs). Existing spatial VLMs often specialize in specific answer formats, such as categorical spatial relations, metric distances, or motion trajectories. This specialization, which we call interface lock-in, limits generalization across different spatial reasoning tasks. To address this challenge, ChronoReplay organizes heterogeneous spatial supervision into chronologically ordered episodes, preserves task-specific answer formats, and balances learning across supervision families. This enables a single model to learn complementary spatial capabilities while maintaining temporal consistency. Key Highlights: Unified Spatial Learning: Supports categorical, metric, and trajectory-based spatial reasoning within a single model. Chronological Replay: Preserves temporal dependencies by organizing training examples into ordered interaction episodes. Family-Balanced Training: Improves cross-task generalization by balancing heterogeneous supervision signals. Strong Benchmark Performance: Achieves consistent improvements across OVO-S-Bench, OST-Bench, and UCS-Bench, including a 13.41-point improvement on OST-Bench. Efficient Streaming Inference: Adaptive frame selection further improves performance while reducing visual processing costs. ChronoReplay demonstrates that effective streaming spatial intelligence requires preserving complementary spatial information across tasks, learning from temporally structured experiences, and selecting relevant visual evidence at inference time.

title: ThinkWorld: World Imagination Reinforces Chain-of-Dynamics Reasoning

details.title: ThinkWorld: World Imagination Reinforces Chain-of-Dynamics Reasoning
details.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have made substantial progress in robotic manipulation, but their generalization remains constrained by the diversity and coverage of action-labeled robot demonstrations. Human videos provide much broader behavioral and environmental experience, while learning from them faces a fundamental trade-off between scalable data and explicit action grounding. We introduce ThinkWorld , a VLA learning framework that grounds action reasoning in world dynamics and strengthens it through reinforcement learning with world imagination. ThinkWorld represents each action thought as a Chain-of-Dynamics (CoD), a sequence of discrete motion tokens that captures the intermediate dynamics connecting the current world to a future state and serves as a common action representation across embodiments. We first initialize CoD with action-labeled demonstrations, then predict the future induced by each CoD and reinforce those whose predictions better match the observed outcome. This enables videos without action annotations to provide direct supervision from observed state transitions, allowing human and robot experience to refine the same reasoning space. Experiments in simulation and on real robots demonstrate effective human-to-robot transfer and strong generalization to unseen tasks and environments.

title: HABIT-Bench: Evaluating Habit Induction from Longitudinal Weak Evidence in Agent Memory

details.title: HABIT-Bench: Evaluating Habit Induction from Longitudinal Weak Evidence in Agent Memory
details.abstract: Hi everyone! I'm one of the authors of HABIT-Bench 👋 Can an agent learn your habits without being explicitly told—and know when not to apply them? Remembering a past choice is not enough. An agent needs to distinguish a recurring habit from a one-off exception, recognize when habits change, and avoid treating its own suggestions as the user's preferences. We introduce HABIT-Bench to evaluate this ability across food, finance, software, and travel. It uses synthetic user histories spanning hundreds of sessions. The tasks require agents to piece together scattered, incomplete evidence and select an appropriate action for a new request—not simply recall something the user explicitly stated. We evaluate eight memory methods with Qwen3-235B-A22B and GLM-5.3-Flash. The best memory-method configuration reaches 33.61% macro accuracy on four-choice tasks, compared with 25% for random guessing . Even when annotated evidence is provided directly, substantial errors remain: finding relevant history is only part of the challenge. Remembering what happened is not the same as understanding what should guide the next decision. 💻 Code: https://github.com/LUMIA-Group/habit-bench 🤗 Dataset: https://huggingface.co/datasets/hollyming/HABIT-Bench We'd love to hear your thoughts, discuss the findings, and see how other memory systems perform on HABIT-Bench!

title: CodeCap-Bench: Can Code Serve as a Good Video Caption?

details.title: CodeCap-Bench: Can Code Serve as a Good Video Caption?
details.abstract: Video captioning aims to preserve visual information through compact descriptions, predominantly using natural language. However, precisely expressing fine-grained spatial structures and temporal dynamics in natural language often leads to lengthy and potentially ambiguous descriptions. In this work, we explore Code as Video Caption, a paradigm where executable programs serve as a complementary representation of visual content through graphical primitives, layout rules, and functions of time. To examine whether code captions effectively preserve video information, we compare them with natural language captions on downstream question answering and video reconstruction tasks. Our results show that code captions achieve superior reasoning accuracy and reconstruction fidelity. Despite these advantages, realizing the potential of code captioning depends on whether current multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can generate faithful code captions. To systematically assess this capability, we introduce CodeCap-Bench, which comprises 323 videos spanning five categories of structured 2D content, along with fine-grained annotations and a multi-level evaluation framework. Extensive experiments reveal that while leading proprietary MLLMs demonstrate promising code captioning capabilities, they still struggle to faithfully capture complex temporal dynamics, with open-source models lagging substantially behind.

title: Can Test-Time Memory Evolution Outperform Test-Time Training for Scientific Discovery?

details.title: Can Test-Time Memory Evolution Outperform Test-Time Training for Scientific Discovery?
details.abstract: Recent test-time training (TTT) frameworks have enabled open-weight large language models (LLMs) to outperform inference-only frameworks powered by frontier models on scientific discovery tasks. However, TTT introduces additional computational cost for online weight updates during the discovery process, making computational efficiency an important consideration when scaling to larger models. This motivates us to explore an efficient test-time adaptation method for scientific discovery. We introduce Test-Time Memory Evolution (TTME), a plug-and-play test-time adaptation method, as an alternative to TTT. TTME continually updates the external memory by distilling the experience to guide subsequent discovery without updating model weights. To have a clean comparison, we evaluate TTME and TTT under the same discovery framework, replacing only the test-time adaptation method.  Our evaluation shows that TTME outperforms TTT on all five mathematical tasks, while reducing computational cost by 82.8-84.6% in FLOPs and 47.7-58.4% in runtime. These results establish TTME as an effective and computationally efficient alternative to TTT in the evaluated discovery settings.

title: RSI Arena: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement with Human Feedback

details.title: RSI Arena: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement with Human Feedback
details.abstract: Can AI agents autonomously train useful language models and improve them using feedback from users? We introduce RSI Arena, a two-stage study of autonomous post-training as a step toward recursive self-improvement. Ten frontier models act as training agents, each starting from NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Lightning 30B-A3B Base. During a six-day first stage, each agent has 1,000 GPU-hours and $300 in API credit on a shared 64-GPU cluster, independently selecting data, implementing training procedures, and choosing checkpoints. We evaluate their models on 20 benchmarks and through blind human evaluations. All ten agents produce working assistants, with the strongest model, trained by GPT-6 Astra, closing a median of 76% of the base-to-Instruct gap across 12 capability benchmarks. Its human-preference rating is also close to NVIDIA Instruct after statistical adjustment for answer length and formatting. In Stage 2, each agent receives the comparison records and votes involving its Stage 1 model and is given three additional days for further training. Using NVIDIA Instruct as a common reference across the two evaluation rounds, we observe an improvement from Stage 1 to Stage 2 in the style-adjusted relative rating of eight of the ten models. We show that benchmark gains were modest, with no clear link to preference gains, while some agents encouraged longer responses and one model showed increased harmful compliance on StrongREJECT. RSI Arena provides an auditable setting for studying how human feedback can guide autonomous model development. It takes a step toward recursive self-improvement with human feedback (RSIHF), in which people help define what improvement means for the AI systems they use.

title: Cross-modal Steering Vectors Exist Across Both Image and Text Generation

details.title: Cross-modal Steering Vectors Exist Across Both Image and Text Generation

title: What Effort Level Should I Choose? On the Economics of Reasoning Effort in LLM Agents

details.title: What Effort Level Should I Choose? On the Economics of Reasoning Effort in LLM Agents
details.abstract: Generative models increasingly expose a reasoning effort setting that lets users scale inference-time compute, trading higher cost for potentially improved performance. Users must choose an effort level before knowing whether extra reasoning will help, and even a successful run does not reveal whether the effort purchased was necessary. Reasoning effort is therefore a credence good: buyers observe the outcome but cannot assess the marginal value of the computation they paid for. In this work, we measure the counterfactual effect of effort levels on both proprietary and open-weight models on four benchmarks, spanning single-call reasoning and long-horizon agentic tasks. Effort, it turns out, does not consistently preserve tasks that lower effort solves, can overspend, and can change trajectory behavior. First, we find that although higher effort can raise accuracy in aggregate, it frequently fails on tasks that lower effort solved. Second, on the subset of easy tasks that every effort level solves, higher effort is generally more costly, with the highest effort level costing up to 42x as much as the lowest. Lastly, effort changes not only how many tokens are used, but also how agents solve tasks: at higher effort, agents verify their own work more heavily and more often search for solutions than work through problems directly, both of which lengthen trajectories without necessarily altering the outcome. These findings show that naively choosing the highest level is not only cost-inefficient but also offers no guarantee of the best instance-level performance. A simple alternative, starting at the lowest effort and escalating only after a verified failure, matches or improves on fixed top effort across all models and benchmarks at lower cost for most proprietary models.

title: Vision-Language-Action or World-Action? Just Action Models

details.title: Vision-Language-Action or World-Action? Just Action Models
details.abstract: We introduce Just Action Models (JAM): action policies trained with a foresight loss on frozen features of recorded future observations, without image or video generation during training or inference. JAM supports generator, vision-language and self-supervised backbones. With cached targets, it reduces estimated online training FLOPs per sample per update by 73% relative to FastWAM. The attached trailer gives an overview of the method and results.

title: Learning and Reasoning with Geometry: How Generation Helps Spatial Understanding

details.title: Learning and Reasoning with Geometry: How Generation Helps Spatial Understanding
details.abstract: Image and video generators can produce spatially consistent visual content, but how to use this capability to improve spatial understanding remains underexplored. We study this problem from two perspectives: geometric supervision during training and explicit geometric evidence during inference. To this end, we introduce a unified geometric understanding and generation model (GeoUG) that integrates depth and multi-view generation with spatial understanding. First, we design a multi-scale depth codec that enables metric-depth generation using a pretrained visual autoencoder, and show that joint training yields task-dependent gains in spatial understanding. Second, we introduce 3DCueBench to control geometric difficulty while balancing selected 2D cues, and find that generated depth provides larger reasoning gains on questions requiring fine-grained geometric discrimination. Building on this finding, we develop adaptive interleaved reasoning, in which GeoUG first drafts an answer and then decides whether to generate geometric evidence to confirm or revise it. We train this decision through reinforcement learning, balancing accuracy gains over retaining the draft against generation cost. GeoUG achieves circular accuracies of 97.9%, 90.8%, and 94.2% on CV-Bench-3D, 3DCueBench, and DA-2K with fewer generation calls than always generating.

title: Harness-Model Collaboration for Long-Horizon Continual Learning

details.title: Harness-Model Collaboration for Long-Horizon Continual Learning
details.abstract: We propose HaMo, a Harness-Model collaborative framework for continual learning in long-horizon agents. Our method separates adaptation into two tightly coupled processes. At the harness level, each trajectory is distilled into a compact experience card containing the task context, initial conditions, and a strategy-level solution outline. These cards are stored in a persistent non-parametric memory, making newly acquired procedural knowledge immediately available to future tasks. At the model level, HaMo continually updates a single parameter-efficient adapter using selected trajectories together with historical replay, improving the model’s ability to exploit accumulated experience while preserving previously acquired capabilities.

title: On the SPOT: Enhancing Speculative Decoding for Diffusion Language Models via Commit-Order Prediction

details.title: On the SPOT: Enhancing Speculative Decoding for Diffusion Language Models via Commit-Order Prediction
details.abstract: Diffusion LMs already know most of the next tokens. What they miss is the order. SPOT learns it. Exact decoding of a diffusion LM fills one masked position per pass. The model's predictions from the previous pass already give the right token at over 90% of positions, but not which position comes next. SPOT is a 0.62M-parameter drafter that predicts this order from the target's own output distributions. The target checks a whole tree of candidates in one forward pass, and coupled-noise match keeps the output exact at any temperature. Up to 6.8× fewer target passes and up to 3.4× the throughput of standard decoding on SDAR-8B Matches or beats calibrated and training-free drafting baselines in every task and budget, at T = 0 and T = 1 The learned drafter transfers across six diffusion LMs New in v2, SPOT-Sets drafts whole commit sets for dynamic threshold decoding. Its exact mode keeps the threshold decoder's output and reaches 7.6× the throughput of standard decoding on SDAR-8B, against 5.0× for the threshold decoder alone (7.9× with max-commit) Code, drafters and a Colab demo are open. title: PhysEvolve: Verifier-grounded Self-evolution for Physical Reasoning with Executable Worlds

details.title: PhysEvolve: Verifier-grounded Self-evolution for Physical Reasoning with Executable Worlds
details.abstract: Physical reasoning underpins how embodied systems understand and act in the physical world, yet vision-language models (VLMs) remain unreliable on questions about dynamics and physical causality. Progress is critically constrained by the scarcity of grounded counterfactual training data, as observational videos capture only the factual trajectory that occurred. The self-evolving paradigm offers a route beyond fixed datasets by enabling models to construct their own training problems. Extending this paradigm to physics, however, requires an external source of truth that can both validate model-proposed environments and verify alternative physical outcomes under intervention. We introduce \physevolve{}, a verifier-grounded self-evolving framework that trains VLMs for causal physical reasoning from model-proposed executable worlds and simulation-authored tasks. At each round, a shared VLM proposes executable world programs and evidence schemas; a deterministic physics engine freezes each valid world, simulates matched baseline and body-elided counterfactual branches, and synthesizes discrete, answer-bound visual tasks. Exact verifier feedback from task solving updates both the shared policy via GRPO and an adaptive curriculum over physical intents. Starting from Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct, \physevolve{} achieves targeted gains across PhysBench, CausalPhys, and ContPhy without human intervention data, improving PhysBench Throwing by $8.8$ points and ContPhy Counterfactual Removal and Goal-Pit by $7.4$ and $24.4$ points. These gains concentrate on interaction-sensitive and altered-world questions, demonstrating zero-shot transfer of causal principles to unseen complex dynamics (cloth, fluid, soft bodies) and real-world video.
